stemMd:
> Some have proposed that hearings in the criminal courts be broadcast live, so that citizens can see justice being done. But witnesses who know they are being filmed tend to perform for the audience instead of answering the questions put to them, and a trial that turns its witnesses into performers serves public curiosity at the expense of the fairness owed to the parties. The openness of justice is better secured by publishing every reasoned judgment promptly, so that anyone can examine what the court decided and why.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Broadcasting hearings live would make every criminal trial unfair to the parties.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Prompt publication of reasoned judgments secures open justice better than live broadcasts.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Witnesses who know that they are being filmed tend to perform for the audience.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Citizens have no legitimate interest in seeing how criminal trials are conducted.

explanationMd:
To find a main conclusion, ask of each sentence: *is this offered as a reason for something else, or is it what the reasons are for?*

- The first sentence reports a proposal (broadcasting hearings) and its aim (letting citizens see justice done). It is the position under attack, not the author's conclusion.
- The second sentence gives the reasons against it: filmed witnesses perform, and performance costs the parties fairness. These are premises.
- The third sentence says what the author recommends instead and claims it does the job better: prompt publication of reasoned judgments secures openness better than broadcasting would.

The reasons in the second sentence are there to support that final comparative claim. So the main conclusion is that prompt publication of reasoned judgments secures open justice better than live broadcasts.

**How to check.** Put "therefore" in front of the candidate and the reasons before it: *filmed witnesses perform, and that costs the parties fairness; therefore publishing reasoned judgments promptly is the better way to secure open justice.* It reads naturally. Put "therefore" in front of the claim about witnesses performing and the argument runs backwards — that claim is offered as a reason, not reached as a result.

distractorRationale.c: This is a premise. The tendency of filmed witnesses to perform is offered as a reason against broadcasting, which in turn supports the author's recommendation; it is not the point the argument is driving at.
distractorRationale.d: The author accepts that openness of justice matters and proposes a better way to secure it. Denying that citizens have any legitimate interest contradicts the argument rather than summarising it.
distractorRationale.a: This overstates a premise. The argument says filmed witnesses "tend to" perform and that this costs the parties fairness; it does not claim every broadcast trial would be unfair, and in any case this concern is a reason for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.

accessibilityText: A conclusion question. The argument says: some have proposed that hearings in the criminal courts be broadcast live, so that citizens can see justice being done; but witnesses who know they are being filmed tend to perform for the audience instead of answering the questions, and a trial that turns its witnesses into performers serves public curiosity at the expense of the fairness owed to the parties; the openness of justice is better secured by publishing every reasoned judgment promptly, so that anyone can examine what the court decided and why. The question asks which statement best expresses the main conclusion. The four answer options are: witnesses who know that they are being filmed tend to perform for the audience; prompt publication of reasoned judgments secures open justice better than live broadcasts; citizens have no legitimate interest in seeing how criminal trials are conducted; broadcasting hearings live would make every criminal trial unfair to the parties.

provenance.notes: Original main-conclusion item in which the argument opens with an opposing proposal, gives premises against it and ends on a comparative recommendation. Distractors are a premise, a contradiction and an overstated intermediate claim.
